Sharp bounds for posterior causal attribution
given complete factual records

Liyao Zhou and Xinwei Sun Email: liyaozhou04@gmail.com
Summary

This supplementary material contains the technical proofs of all theoretical results in the main paper, details of the rules for selecting active probabilities, regularized margin estimators, and directional inference procedures, and complete derivations for the numerical and empirical studies. Additional examples on multilevel mediation, ordinal exposures, and reliability networks are also provided.

Some key words: Causes of effects; Credal network; Partial identification; Probability of necessity; Response coupling; Sharp bound; Structural causal model.

1 Introduction

Retrospective causal attribution asks which earlier events contributed to an observed adverse outcome. When an industrial reactor shuts down following both a cooling fault and abnormal feed composition, evaluating whether repairing the cooling valve would have prevented that specific incident requires retrospective analysis beyond population-level intervention effects. Such questions belong to the causes-of-effects framework (Pearl, 1999; Tian & Pearl, 2000; Dawid & Musio, 2022).

Observational distributions determine marginal potential-response probabilities at fixed input settings, whereas retrospective attribution depends on cross-world associations between potential responses under alternative inputs. In multistage systems, this unidentifiability propagates sequentially through intermediate variables. A complete factual record provides direct structural information by fixing the realized response of every constituent mechanism and restricting the conditional distributions of its remaining counterfactual responses.

Partial-identification bounds have been established for probabilities of causation and mediated attribution (Dawid et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025), and posterior causal effects are point identified under binary monotonicity (Lu et al., 2023). General structural causal models also admit credal-network representations for counterfactual bounding (Zaffalon et al., 2020). Across these settings, marginal optimization yields sharp bounds whenever locally admissible conditional response distributions across distinct mechanisms and parent configurations can be realized simultaneously within a single compatible structural causal model.

In finite Markovian models under complete factual conditioning, mutual independence of exogenous disturbances preserves posterior independence across mechanisms and restricts each nonfactual response distribution to a capped probability simplex. Conditioning on the realized response at each node combines any collection of locally feasible distributions into a single compatible model. This joint attainability yields sharp attribution bounds for multistage interventions and mediated effects, and accommodates structural restrictions through compatible joint response distributions. The resulting product structure supports greedy backward recursion along causal chains, exact vertex enumeration across shared mechanisms in general directed acyclic graphs, and root-nn consistent plug-in estimation with finite-sample and asymptotic confidence intervals.

2 Model and posterior distributions

This section formulates the retrospective attribution target in a finite Markovian structural causal model and characterizes the conditional response distributions given a complete factual record.

2.1 Model and attribution target

Let V=(V1,…,Vd)V=(V_{1},\ldots,V_{d}) be causally ordered variables with finite state spaces 𝒳j\mathcal{X}_{j}. Write 𝒱={V1,…,Vd}\mathcal{V}=\{V_{1},\ldots,V_{d}\} and 𝒳B=∏Vj∈B𝒳j\mathcal{X}_{B}=\prod_{V_{j}\in B}\mathcal{X}_{j} for B⊆𝒱B\subseteq\mathcal{V}. The parents of VjV_{j} are Pa⁡(Vj)⊆{V1,…,Vj−1}\Pa(V_{j})\subseteq\{V_{1},\ldots,V_{j-1}\}, with configuration space 𝒫j=𝒳Pa⁡(Vj)\mathcal{P}_{j}=\mathcal{X}_{\Pa(V_{j})}. Let Pj=VPa⁡(Vj)P_{j}=V_{\Pa(V_{j})} be the random parent vector and Vj​(p)V_{j}(p) the potential response at p∈𝒫jp\in\mathcal{P}_{j}. The structural equations follow a Markovian causal model.

Assumption 1.

For j=1,…,dj=1,\ldots,d, Vj=fj​(Pj,Uj)V_{j}=f_{j}(P_{j},U_{j}), where the exogenous disturbances U1,…,UdU_{1},\ldots,U_{d} are mutually independent.

Under Assumption 1, the response vectors Rj={Vj​(p)}p∈𝒫jR_{j}=\{V_{j}(p)\}_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{j}} are mutually independent across j=1,…,dj=1,\ldots,d. For every p∈𝒫jp\in\mathcal{P}_{j} with pr⁡(Pj=p)>0\pr(P_{j}=p)>0, consistency gives

μj(w;p)=pr{Vj(p)=w}=pr(Vj=w∣Pj=p).\mu_{j}(w;p)=\pr\{V_{j}(p)=w\}=\pr(V_{j}=w\mid P_{j}=p).

Write μj​(p)={μj​(w,p):w∈𝒳j}\mu_{j}(p)=\{\mu_{j}(w;p):w\in\mathcal{X}_{j}\}. Observational positivity, pr⁡(Pj=p)>0\pr(P_{j}=p)>0, is required only at parent configurations entering the attribution functional or the structural compatibility constraints introduced in § 3.

Fix a complete factual record V=vV=v with pr⁡(V=v)>0\pr(V=v)>0, let pj⋆=vPa⁡(Vj)p_{j}^{\star}=v_{\Pa(V_{j})} denote the observed parent configuration of VjV_{j}, and take Y=VdY=V_{d} as the outcome. For an intervention set A⊆𝒱∖{Y}A\subseteq\mathcal{V}\setminus\{Y\} and level a∈𝒳Aa\in\mathcal{X}_{A}, let YaY_{a} denote the counterfactual outcome under do⁡(A=a)\mathrm{do}(A=a). Consistency yields YvA=vYY_{v_{A}}=v_{Y} on {V=v}\{V=v\}. For a prespecified score function g:𝒳Y→ℝg:\mathcal{X}_{Y}\to\mathbb{R}, define the posterior attribution effect

τg​(A,a,v)=g⁡(vY)−E⁡{g⁡(Ya)∣V=v}.\tau_{g}(A,a;v)=g(v_{Y})-E\{g(Y_{a})\mid V=v\}. (1)

When A={X}A=\{X\}, write τg​(a,v)=τg​({X},a,v)\tau_{g}(a;v)=\tau_{g}(\{X\},a;v). For binary XX and YY with vX=vY=1v_{X}=v_{Y}=1, a=0a=0, and g⁡(y)=yg(y)=y, the target in (1) equals the posterior total causal effect 1−pr⁡(Y0=1∣V=v)1-\pr(Y_{0}=1\mid V=v) (Lu et al., 2023).

Consider the binary chain X→M→YX\to M\to Y at the factual record v=(1,1,1)v=(1,1,1) under do⁡(X=0)\mathrm{do}(X=0). Write u=pr⁡{M⁡(0)=1∣V=v}u=\pr\{M(0)=1\mid V=v\} and r=pr⁡{Y⁡(0)=1∣V=v}r=\pr\{Y(0)=1\mid V=v\}. Conditional independence of the two response mechanisms and consistency Y⁡(1)=1Y(1)=1 yield

pr⁡(Y0=1∣V=v)=u+(1−u)​r.\pr(Y_{0}=1\mid V=v)=u+(1-u)r.

Suppose pr⁡(M=1∣X=1)=0.6\pr(M=1\mid X=1)=0.6, pr⁡(M=1∣X=0)=0.3\pr(M=1\mid X=0)=0.3, pr⁡(Y=1∣M=1)=0.8\pr(Y=1\mid M=1)=0.8, and pr⁡(Y=1∣M=0)=0.2\pr(Y=1\mid M=0)=0.2. Dividing the joint probability bounds pr⁡{M⁡(0)=1,M⁡(1)=1}≤0.3\pr\{M(0)=1,M(1)=1\}\leq 0.3 and pr⁡{Y⁡(0)=1,Y⁡(1)=1}≤0.2\pr\{Y(0)=1,Y(1)=1\}\leq 0.2 by the factual probabilities 0.60.6 and 0.80.8 restricts uu to [0,0.5][0,0.5] and rr to [0,0.25][0,0.25]. Joint attainability of these intervals yields pr⁡(Y0=1∣V=v)∈[0,0.625]\pr(Y_{0}=1\mid V=v)\in[0,0.625] and τg​(0,v)∈[0.375,1]\tau_{g}(0;v)\in[0.375,1].

2.2 Local posterior bounds and joint attainability

Let αj=μj​(vj,pj⋆)\alpha_{j}=\mu_{j}(v_{j};p_{j}^{\star}) denote the factual response probability at node jj, and write qj​(w,p)=pr⁡{Vj​(p)=w∣V=v}q_{j}(w;p)=\pr\{V_{j}(p)=w\mid V=v\} with conditional probability vector qj​(p)={qj​(w,p):w∈𝒳j}q_{j}(p)=\{q_{j}(w;p):w\in\mathcal{X}_{j}\}. For any nonfactual parent configuration p≠pj⋆p\neq p_{j}^{\star}, the joint probability inequality αj​qj​(w,p)≤μj​(w,p)\alpha_{j}q_{j}(w;p)\leq\mu_{j}(w;p) restricts qj​(p)q_{j}(p) to the capped probability simplex

𝒦j(p)={q∈Δ(𝒳j):αjq(w)≤μj(w;p),w∈𝒳j}.\mathcal{K}_{j}(p)=\{q\in\Delta(\mathcal{X}_{j}):\alpha_{j}q(w)\leq\mu_{j}(w;p),\ w\in\mathcal{X}_{j}\}. (2)

At the factual configuration, consistency fixes 𝒦j​(pj⋆)={δvj}\mathcal{K}_{j}(p_{j}^{\star})=\{\delta_{v_{j}}\}. Because the factual record vv remains fixed throughout, it is suppressed in the notation for feasible sets. The following theorem establishes posterior independence across mechanisms and the joint attainability of these local bounds.

Theorem 1.

Under Assumption 1, fix the marginal distributions {μj​(p)}\{\mu_{j}(p)\} and a complete record V=vV=v with pr⁡(V=v)>0\pr(V=v)>0. Then:

  • (i)

    R1,…,RdR_{1},\ldots,R_{d} are mutually independent given V=vV=v, with each conditional distribution determined by Vj​(pj⋆)=vjV_{j}(p_{j}^{\star})=v_{j};

  • (ii)

    the feasible set of qj​(p)q_{j}(p) is 𝒦j​(p)\mathcal{K}_{j}(p) for every jj and pp;

  • (iii)

    every collection of conditional distributions qj​(p)∈𝒦j​(p)q_{j}(p)\in\mathcal{K}_{j}(p) across all jj and pp is jointly attained by a single compatible Markovian structural causal model.

The factual event {V=v}=⋂j=1d{Vj(pj⋆)=vj}\{V=v\}=\bigcap_{j=1}^{d}\{V_{j}(p_{j}^{\star})=v_{j}\} conditions each independent response vector on its own realized response, giving pr⁡(V=v)=∏j=1dαj\pr(V=v)=\prod_{j=1}^{d}\alpha_{j}. When αj<1\alpha_{j}<1, any selection qj​(p)∈𝒦j​(p)q_{j}(p)\in\mathcal{K}_{j}(p) defines a residual distribution rj​(p)={μj​(p)−αj​qj​(p)}/(1−αj)∈Δ⁡(𝒳j)r_{j}(p)=\{\mu_{j}(p)-\alpha_{j}q_{j}(p)\}/(1-\alpha_{j})\in\Delta(\mathcal{X}_{j}) for p≠pj⋆p\neq p_{j}^{\star}. Taking the nonfactual responses to be conditionally independent given Vj​(pj⋆)V_{j}(p_{j}^{\star}), with conditional distribution qj​(p)q_{j}(p) on {Vj(pj⋆)=vj}\{V_{j}(p_{j}^{\star})=v_{j}\} and rj​(p)r_{j}(p) on {Vj(pj⋆)≠vj}\{V_{j}(p_{j}^{\star})\neq v_{j}\}, matches all marginal distributions and realizes the selected posterior distributions simultaneously (§ S1.1 of the Supplementary Material).

Conditioning on a partial factual record can induce dependence across mechanisms. In the binary chain M→YM\to Y with M=UMM=U_{M}, Y⁡(m)=I⁡(m=UY)Y(m)=I(m=U_{Y}), and independent Bernoulli⁡(1/2)\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2) disturbances UMU_{M} and UYU_{Y}, the event {Y=1}={UM=UY}\{Y=1\}=\{U_{M}=U_{Y}\} yields pr⁡(UM=1,UY=1∣Y=1)=1/2≠pr⁡(UM=1∣Y=1)​pr⁡(UY=1∣Y=1)=1/4\pr(U_{M}=1,U_{Y}=1\mid Y=1)=1/2\neq\pr(U_{M}=1\mid Y=1)\pr(U_{Y}=1\mid Y=1)=1/4. Observing the complete record (M,Y)=(1,1)(M,Y)=(1,1) fixes UM=UY=1U_{M}=U_{Y}=1 and restores posterior independence.

3 Sharp attribution bounds

Combining the local posterior sets across mechanisms yields sharp identification intervals for multistage interventions, mediated effects, and models subject to cross-world structural restrictions.

3.1 Main result and binary cases

For a collection of conditional distributions q={qj​(p)}q=\{q_{j}(p)\}, define

Ψg(q;A,a)=∑z∈𝒳𝒱:zA=ag(zY)∏j:Vj∉Aqj(zj;zPa⁡(Vj)),𝒦A=∏j:Vj∉A∏p∈𝒫j𝒦j(p).\Psi_{g}(q;A,a)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}z\in\mathcal{X}_{\mathcal{V}}:\\ z_{A}=a\end{subarray}}g(z_{Y})\prod_{j:V_{j}\notin A}q_{j}(z_{j};z_{\Pa(V_{j})}),\qquad\mathcal{K}_{A}=\prod_{j:V_{j}\notin A}\prod_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{j}}\mathcal{K}_{j}(p). (3)

Theorem 1 gives E⁡{g⁡(Ya)∣V=v}=Ψg​(q,A,a)E\{g(Y_{a})\mid V=v\}=\Psi_{g}(q;A,a). Write Lg=Lg​(A,a,v)L_{g}=L_{g}(A,a;v) and Ug=Ug​(A,a,v)U_{g}=U_{g}(A,a;v) for the endpoints

[Lg,Ug]=[g(vY)−maxq∈𝒦AΨg(q;A,a),g(vY)−minq∈𝒦AΨg(q;A,a)].[L_{g},U_{g}]=\left[g(v_{Y})-\max_{q\in\mathcal{K}_{A}}\Psi_{g}(q;A,a),\quad g(v_{Y})-\min_{q\in\mathcal{K}_{A}}\Psi_{g}(q;A,a)\right]. (4)

Joint attainability over the product domain 𝒦A\mathcal{K}_{A} establishes the sharpness of these posterior attribution bounds.

Theorem 2.

Under Assumption 1, if the marginal distributions entering (3) are identified and pr⁡(V=v)>0\pr(V=v)>0, the sharp identified interval for τg​(A,a,v)\tau_{g}(A,a;v) is [Lg​(A,a,v),Ug​(A,a,v)][L_{g}(A,a;v),U_{g}(A,a;v)], and every value in this interval is attained by a compatible Markovian structural causal model.

The attainable expectations form a closed interval because 𝒦A\mathcal{K}_{A} is compact and connected and Ψg\Psi_{g} is continuous. In the binary system X→YX\to Y with (X,Y)=(1,1)(X,Y)=(1,1), a=0a=0, and g⁡(y)=yg(y)=y, the effect τg​(0,v)\tau_{g}(0;v) equals the probability of necessity, and (2) yields the classical Fréchet bounds (Pearl, 1999; Tian & Pearl, 2000):

max⁡{0,1−pr{Y(0)=1}pr{Y(1)=1}}≤pr⁡{Y⁡(0)=0∣Y⁡(1)=1}≤min⁡{1,1−pr{Y(0)=1}pr{Y(1)=1}}.\max\left\{0,1-\frac{\pr\{Y(0)=1\}}{\pr\{Y(1)=1\}}\right\}\leq\pr\{Y(0)=0\mid Y(1)=1\}\leq\min\left\{1,\frac{1-\pr\{Y(0)=1\}}{\pr\{Y(1)=1\}}\right\}.

More generally, suppose XX and all its descendants are binary and each affected structural mechanism is coordinatewise nondecreasing in its affected parents. Every parent configuration p≤pj⋆p\leq p_{j}^{\star} reached under do⁡(X=0)\mathrm{do}(X=0) then satisfies Vj​(p)≤Vj​(pj⋆)V_{j}(p)\leq V_{j}(p_{j}^{\star}) almost surely. The conditional success probability qj​(1,p)q_{j}(1;p) equals 00 for vj=0v_{j}=0 and μj​(1,p)/αj\mu_{j}(1;p)/\alpha_{j} for vj=1v_{j}=1, recovering the point identification result of Lu et al. (2023). When all observed variables equal one, this point-identified effect coincides with the unrestricted lower attribution bound.

Corollary 1.

Suppose all variables are binary, the factual realization is V=𝟏V=\boldsymbol{1}, and the marginal distributions are compatible with coordinatewise nondecreasing structural mechanisms. For A⊆𝒱∖{Y}A\subseteq\mathcal{V}\setminus\{Y\}, a=𝟎Aa=\boldsymbol{0}_{A}, and g⁡(y)=yg(y)=y, the point-identified attribution effect τmono​(A,a,𝟏)\tau_{\mathrm{mono}}(A,a;\boldsymbol{1}) under structural monotonicity satisfies τmono​(A,a,𝟏)=Lg​(A,a,𝟏)\tau_{\mathrm{mono}}(A,a;\boldsymbol{1})=L_{g}(A,a;\boldsymbol{1}).

3.2 Mediated attribution

For a mediator subset 𝒮⊆𝒱∖(A∪{Y})\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{V}\setminus(A\cup\{Y\}), let M=V𝒮M=V_{\mathcal{S}} and write MaM_{a} and Ya,mY_{a,m} for the corresponding counterfactuals. Define the posterior total natural direct effect, pure natural indirect effect, and total natural indirect effect by

τgTNDE\displaystyle\tau_{g}^{\mathrm{TNDE}} =E⁡{g⁡(YvA,MvA)−g⁡(Ya,MvA)∣V=v},\displaystyle=E\{g(Y_{v_{A},M_{v_{A}}})-g(Y_{a,M_{v_{A}}})\mid V=v\},
τgPNIE\displaystyle\tau_{g}^{\mathrm{PNIE}} =E⁡{g⁡(Ya,MvA)−g⁡(Ya,Ma)∣V=v},\displaystyle=E\{g(Y_{a,M_{v_{A}}})-g(Y_{a,M_{a}})\mid V=v\},
τgTNIE\displaystyle\tau_{g}^{\mathrm{TNIE}} =E⁡{g⁡(YvA,MvA)−g⁡(YvA,Ma)∣V=v}.\displaystyle=E\{g(Y_{v_{A},M_{v_{A}}})-g(Y_{v_{A},M_{a}})\mid V=v\}.

Under conditional response distributions q={qj​(p)}q=\{q_{j}(p)\}, consistency MvA=vMM_{v_{A}}=v_{M} and Ya,Ma=YaY_{a,M_{a}}=Y_{a} yield

τgTNDE\displaystyle\tau_{g}^{\mathrm{TNDE}} =g⁡(vY)−Ψg​{q;A∪𝒮,(a,vM)},\displaystyle=g(v_{Y})-\Psi_{g}\{q;A\cup\mathcal{S},(a,v_{M})\},
τgPNIE\displaystyle\tau_{g}^{\mathrm{PNIE}} =Ψg​{q;A∪𝒮,(a,vM)}−Ψg​(q,A,a).\displaystyle=\Psi_{g}\{q;A\cup\mathcal{S},(a,v_{M})\}-\Psi_{g}(q;A,a).

In particular, τgTNDE=τg​{A∪𝒮,(a,vM);v}\tau_{g}^{\mathrm{TNDE}}=\tau_{g}\{A\cup\mathcal{S},(a,v_{M});v\}. For a single mediator M=VmM=V_{m}, conditional independence gives

E⁡{g⁡(YvA,Ma)∣V=v}=∑w∈𝒳mpr⁡(Ma=w∣V=v)​Ψg​{q;A∪{Vm},(vA,w)}.E\{g(Y_{v_{A},M_{a}})\mid V=v\}=\sum_{w\in\mathcal{X}_{m}}\pr(M_{a}=w\mid V=v)\Psi_{g}\{q;A\cup\{V_{m}\},(v_{A},w)\}.

For multiple mediators, the same decomposition holds when no node in 𝒮\mathcal{S} is a descendant of any non-mediator descendant of 𝒮\mathcal{S} outside AA (§ S1.3, Lemma S1). For each mediated effect, minimizing and maximizing the corresponding functional over a common q∈𝒦Aq\in\mathcal{K}_{A} yields the sharp identified interval. Within each compatible model, τg​(A,a,v)=τgTNDE+τgPNIE\tau_{g}(A,a;v)=\tau_{g}^{\mathrm{TNDE}}+\tau_{g}^{\mathrm{PNIE}}, whereas the sharp interval endpoints of the two components are optimized separately over 𝒦A\mathcal{K}_{A}.

3.3 Structural restrictions

Cross-world shape restrictions constrain the response vector RjR_{j} to a specified subset 𝒞j⊆∏p∈𝒫j𝒳j\mathcal{C}_{j}\subseteq\prod_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{j}}\mathcal{X}_{j}, coupling the conditional distributions qj​(p)q_{j}(p) across distinct parent configurations p∈𝒫jp\in\mathcal{P}_{j}. Let 𝒬j\mathcal{Q}_{j} denote the set of collections {qj​(p)}p∈𝒫j\{q_{j}(p)\}_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{j}} induced by conditioning compatible joint response distributions supported on 𝒞j\mathcal{C}_{j} on the factual event {Vj(pj⋆)=vj}\{V_{j}(p_{j}^{\star})=v_{j}\} (§ S2), and define the restricted product domain 𝒬A=∏j:Vj∉A𝒬j\mathcal{Q}_{A}=\prod_{j:V_{j}\notin A}\mathcal{Q}_{j}. In the unrestricted case 𝒞j=∏p∈𝒫j𝒳j\mathcal{C}_{j}=\prod_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{j}}\mathcal{X}_{j}, 𝒬j\mathcal{Q}_{j} reduces to ∏p∈𝒫j𝒦j​(p)\prod_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{j}}\mathcal{K}_{j}(p) and 𝒬A=𝒦A\mathcal{Q}_{A}=\mathcal{K}_{A}. Optimizing over 𝒬A\mathcal{Q}_{A} yields sharp bounds under these structural restrictions.

Theorem 3.

Suppose a compatible joint response distribution supported on 𝒞j\mathcal{C}_{j} exists for every jj. Under Assumption 1, identified marginal distributions, and pr⁡(V=v)>0\pr(V=v)>0, (4) with 𝒬A\mathcal{Q}_{A} in place of 𝒦A\mathcal{K}_{A} gives the sharp identified interval for τg​(A,a,v)\tau_{g}(A,a;v). Every value in this interval is attained by a compatible model satisfying the response restrictions.

For an ordered variable Vj∈{0,…,Mj}V_{j}\in\{0,\ldots,M_{j}\} with an ordered parent X∈{x0<⋯<xK}X\in\{x_{0}<\cdots<x_{K}\} and remaining parent set Sj=Pa⁡(Vj)∖{X}S_{j}=\Pa(V_{j})\setminus\{X\} with configurations s∈𝒳Sjs\in\mathcal{X}_{S_{j}}, bounded adjacent-increment restrictions take the form

0≤Vj​(s,xk+1)−Vj​(s,xk)≤bj​kalmost surely,s∈𝒳Sj,k=0,…,K−1,0\leq V_{j}(s,x_{k+1})-V_{j}(s,x_{k})\leq b_{jk}\quad\text{almost surely},\qquad s\in\mathcal{X}_{S_{j}},\quad k=0,\ldots,K-1, (5)

for given integers bj​k≥0b_{jk}\geq 0. Setting bj​k=Mjb_{jk}=M_{j} imposes monotonicity across the ordered levels of XX at fixed ss, whereas bj​k=1b_{jk}=1 restricts adjacent responses to unit increments. Write Fj​(r,s,xk)=pr⁡(Vj≤r∣Sj=s,X=xk)F_{j}(r;s,x_{k})=\pr(V_{j}\leq r\mid S_{j}=s,X=x_{k}), with Fj​(r,s,xk)=0F_{j}(r;s,x_{k})=0 for r<0r<0 and Fj​(r,s,xk)=1F_{j}(r;s,x_{k})=1 for r≥Mjr\geq M_{j}. The following proposition characterizes marginal compatibility with these adjacent-increment bounds.

Proposition 1.

Let 𝒞j\mathcal{C}_{j} be the set of response vectors satisfying (5). A compatible joint response distribution exists if and only if

Fj​(r,s,xk)≥Fj​(r,s,xk+1)≥Fj​(r−bj​k,s,xk)for all ​s,k,r.F_{j}(r;s,x_{k})\geq F_{j}(r;s,x_{k+1})\geq F_{j}(r-b_{jk};s,x_{k})\qquad\text{for all }s,k,r. (6)

Restrictions relative to the observed response take the form Vj​(p)≤Vj​(pj⋆)V_{j}(p)\leq V_{j}(p_{j}^{\star}) for specified configurations p∈ℰj⊆𝒫j∖{pj⋆}p\in\mathcal{E}_{j}\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{j}\setminus\{p_{j}^{\star}\} ordered below pj⋆p_{j}^{\star}, with the inequality reversed for configurations ordered above pj⋆p_{j}^{\star}. When these are the only comparisons, the conditional distributions can be optimized separately across parent configurations: bivariate distributions for each pair {Vj​(pj⋆),Vj​(p)}\{V_{j}(p_{j}^{\star}),V_{j}(p)\} combine conditional on their common observed response, yielding 𝒬j=∏p𝒬j​(p)\mathcal{Q}_{j}=\prod_{p}\mathcal{Q}_{j}(p), where 𝒬j​(p)\mathcal{Q}_{j}(p) is the set of conditional distributions admitted by that pairwise comparison (Lemma S2).

The five-node mediation network in § S6.1, comprising a binary covariate CC, binary exposure XX, three-level mediators (M1,M2)(M_{1},M_{2}), and binary outcome YY at v=(1,1,3,3,1)v=(1,1,3,3,1), illustrates these restrictions. Imposing monotonicity relative to the observed response on neither mechanism, the outcome alone, the mediators alone, and both mechanisms contracts the sharp interval for the posterior total causal effect τg​(0,v)\tau_{g}(0;v) from [0.200,1.000][0.200,1.000] to [0.200,0.800][0.200,0.800], [0.200,0.570][0.200,0.570], and [0.200,0.452][0.200,0.452], respectively.

4 Exact computation

The multilinear structure of the counterfactual expectation over the product of capped simplices enables exact computation via backward recursion along causal chains and vertex enumeration in general directed acyclic graphs.

4.1 Causal chains

In the unrestricted model, Ψg\Psi_{g} is linear in each conditional response distribution separately, so its extrema occur at products of vertices of 𝒦j​(p)\mathcal{K}_{j}(p). Consider the causal chain Z0=X→Z1→⋯→Zm=YZ_{0}=X\to Z_{1}\to\cdots\to Z_{m}=Y, where any additional parents of Z1,…,ZmZ_{1},\ldots,Z_{m} are unaffected by do⁡(X=a)\mathrm{do}(X=a). Let pj​(s)p_{j}(s) denote the parent configuration of ZjZ_{j} when Zj−1=sZ_{j-1}=s and all additional parents retain their factual values. Backward dynamic programming yields the sharp attribution bounds along the chain.

Corollary 2.

Under Assumption 1, identified marginal probabilities, and pr⁡(V=v)>0\pr(V=v)>0, suppose the affected variables form the chain above without additional response restrictions. Set hm−=hm+=gh_{m}^{-}=h_{m}^{+}=g. For j=m,…,1j=m,\ldots,1 and s∈𝒳Zj−1s\in\mathcal{X}_{Z_{j-1}}, define

hj−1−(s)=minq∈𝒦Zj​{pj​(s)}∑z∈𝒳Zjq(z)hj−(z),hj−1+(s)=maxq∈𝒦Zj​{pj​(s)}∑z∈𝒳Zjq(z)hj+(z).h_{j-1}^{-}(s)=\min_{q\in\mathcal{K}_{Z_{j}}\{p_{j}(s)\}}\sum_{z\in\mathcal{X}_{Z_{j}}}q(z)h_{j}^{-}(z),\qquad h_{j-1}^{+}(s)=\max_{q\in\mathcal{K}_{Z_{j}}\{p_{j}(s)\}}\sum_{z\in\mathcal{X}_{Z_{j}}}q(z)h_{j}^{+}(z). (7)

The sharp interval for τg​(a,v)\tau_{g}(a;v) is [g⁡(vY)−h0+​(a),g⁡(vY)−h0−​(a)][g(v_{Y})-h_{0}^{+}(a),\,g(v_{Y})-h_{0}^{-}(a)].

At a nonfactual configuration in (7), sorting the states by their continuation values and allocating probability successively up to min⁡{1,μZj​[z;pj​(s)]/αZj}\min\{1,\mu_{Z_{j}}[z;p_{j}(s)]/\alpha_{Z_{j}}\} yields the local optimum; ascending order attains the minimum and descending order the maximum. At the factual configuration, the feasible set is a singleton. Distinct predecessor states index distinct parent configurations, so Theorem 1(iii) ensures that the optimizing choices are jointly attainable. With Lj=|𝒳Zj|L_{j}=|\mathcal{X}_{Z_{j}}|, reusing the sorted state order at each stage requires O⁡{∑j=1m(Lj​log⁡Lj+Lj−1​Lj)}O\{\sum_{j=1}^{m}(L_{j}\log L_{j}+L_{j-1}L_{j})\} operations. The explicit allocation rule and proof are given in § S3.1.

4.2 General graphs

In a general directed acyclic graph, reconverging paths can cause distinct counterfactual branches to evaluate a mechanism jj at the same nonfactual parent configuration pp, thereby sharing the conditional distribution qj​(p)q_{j}(p). Let ℛact\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{act}} be the set of nonfactual pairs (j,p)(j,p) with Vj∉AV_{j}\notin A and p≠pj⋆p\neq p_{j}^{\star} entering Ψg​(q,A,a)\Psi_{g}(q;A,a), and let 𝒦jext​(p)\mathcal{K}_{j}^{\mathrm{ext}}(p) denote the vertex set of 𝒦j​(p)\mathcal{K}_{j}(p).

For a selected subset of mechanisms ℱ⊆𝒱∖A\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{V}\setminus A, partition the active nonfactual distributions as q=(qℱ,q−ℱ)q=(q_{\mathcal{F}},q_{-\mathcal{F}}) according to whether Vj∈ℱV_{j}\in\mathcal{F}. Let 𝒦ℱext\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{F}}^{\mathrm{ext}} and 𝒦−ℱext\mathcal{K}_{-\mathcal{F}}^{\mathrm{ext}} denote the corresponding products of the vertex sets 𝒦jext​(p)\mathcal{K}_{j}^{\mathrm{ext}}(p). This decomposition reduces optimization over 𝒦A\mathcal{K}_{A} to outer vertex enumeration over ℱ\mathcal{F} combined with inner optimization over the remaining mechanisms.

Proposition 2.

Under the conditions of Theorem 2, for any selected ℱ\mathcal{F} and opt∈{min,max}\operatorname{opt}\in\{\min,\max\},

optq∈𝒦A​Ψg​(q,A,a)=optqℱ∈𝒦ℱext​optq−ℱ∈𝒦−ℱext​Ψg​(qℱ,q−ℱ,A,a),\underset{q\in\mathcal{K}_{A}}{\operatorname{opt}}\Psi_{g}(q;A,a)=\underset{q_{\mathcal{F}}\in\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{F}}^{\mathrm{ext}}}{\operatorname{opt}}\,\underset{q_{-\mathcal{F}}\in\mathcal{K}_{-\mathcal{F}}^{\mathrm{ext}}}{\operatorname{opt}}\Psi_{g}(q_{\mathcal{F}},q_{-\mathcal{F}};A,a),

where factual conditional distributions remain fixed at qj​(pj⋆)=δvjq_{j}(p_{j}^{\star})=\delta_{v_{j}}. Whenever a fixed outer selection leaves a non-negative weighted sum of components involving disjoint sets of free conditional distributions, those components can be optimized separately, with chain components evaluated via Corollary 2.

In the reactor graph of Fig. 1(a), recording TT in the parent sets of both PP and YY separates all downstream conditional distributions across branches, permitting direct backward recursion with ℱ=∅\mathcal{F}=\emptyset.

In the binary diamond network of Fig. 1(b) with v=(1,0,0,1)v=(1,0,0,1), pr{B(1)=0}=1\pr\{B(1)=0\}=1, pr{B(0)=1}=pr{C(1)=1}=pr{C(0)=1}=1/2\pr\{B(0)=1\}=\pr\{C(1)=1\}=\pr\{C(0)=1\}=1/2, and Y⁡(b,c)=I⁡(b=c)Y(b,c)=I(b=c), both branches b∈{0,1}b\in\{0,1\} of BB under do⁡(X=0)\mathrm{do}(X=0) share qC​(0)∈Δ⁡({0,1})q_{C}(0)\in\Delta(\{0,1\}). Optimizing qC​(0)q_{C}(0) separately across the two branches yields [0,1][0,1] for pr⁡(Y0=1∣V=v)\pr(Y_{0}=1\mid V=v), whereas holding qC​(0)q_{C}(0) fixed across branches gives {qC​(0,0)+qC​(1,0)}/2=1/2\{q_{C}(0;0)+q_{C}(1;0)\}/2=1/2, which is recovered by selecting ℱ={C}\mathcal{F}=\{C\} (§ S3.2).

5 Estimation and inference

Replacing the population marginal distributions with sample estimates yields plug-in estimators for the sharp attribution bounds, whose polyhedral structure supports both finite-sample simultaneous confidence intervals and asymptotic directional inference.

5.1 Estimation of sharp bounds

Let 𝒟A\mathcal{D}_{A} denote the feasible posterior domain, equal to 𝒦A\mathcal{K}_{A} in the unrestricted model and 𝒬A\mathcal{Q}_{A} under response restrictions. Replacing μ\mu by an estimator μ^\widehat{\mu} defines the plug-in domain 𝒟^A\widehat{\mathcal{D}}_{A}, over which optimizing the endpoint functionals yields (L^g,U^g)(\widehat{L}_{g},\widehat{U}_{g}). In the unrestricted model, empirical or survey-weighted conditional frequencies give estimates in the product of probability simplices.

For ordered parents, fused least-squares estimation with tuning parameter γn≥0\gamma_{n}\geq 0 penalizes L1L_{1} differences between adjacent conditional distributions (Gneiting & Raftery, 2007; Tibshirani et al., 2005). Let ℳj\mathcal{M}_{j} be the set of marginal probability tables admitted by joint response distributions on 𝒞j\mathcal{C}_{j}. Compatibility is enforced directly during constrained fused estimation or by projecting preliminary estimates μ~j\widetilde{\mu}_{j} onto ℳj\mathcal{M}_{j} with fixed positive-definite quadratic weights WjW_{j} (§ S4.1). Under fixed positive parent-cell probabilities, the fused estimator satisfies ∥μ^j−μj∥∞=Op(n−1/2+γn)\|\widehat{\mu}_{j}-\mu_{j}\|_{\infty}=O_{p}(n^{-1/2}+\gamma_{n}) and differs from the unpenalized constrained estimator by Op​(γn)O_{p}(\gamma_{n}), achieving first-order equivalence when n​γn→0\sqrt{n}\gamma_{n}\to 0 (Knight & Fu, 2000) (Lemma S3).

For fixed (A,a)(A,a), vv, gg, and {𝒞j}\{\mathcal{C}_{j}\}, let ℐ\mathcal{I} be the prespecified set of m=|ℐ|m=|\mathcal{I}| active scalar probabilities entering the target functional or coupled to those probabilities through the response restrictions 𝒞j\mathcal{C}_{j}. Write ‖μ^−μ‖ℐ=max(j,p,w)∈ℐ⁡|μ^j​(w,p)−μj​(w,p)|\|\widehat{\mu}-\mu\|_{\mathcal{I}}=\max_{(j,p,w)\in\mathcal{I}}|\widehat{\mu}_{j}(w;p)-\mu_{j}(w;p)|. For an unrestricted outcome mechanism and g⁡(y)=I⁡(y=vY)g(y)=I(y=v_{Y}), collapsing outcome categories retains only μY​(vY,p)\mu_{Y}(v_{Y};p); the equality of the resulting extrema is proved in § S4.2. The following theorem establishes the stability and convergence rate of the plug-in endpoint estimators.

Theorem 4.

Fix finite state spaces and response sets {𝒞j}\{\mathcal{C}_{j}\}, with μj∈ℳj\mu_{j}\in\mathcal{M}_{j} for every jj. Let μ^j∈ℳj\widehat{\mu}_{j}\in\mathcal{M}_{j} be obtained by constrained fused least squares or weighted quadratic projection. If ‖μ^−μ‖ℐ=op​(1)\|\widehat{\mu}-\mu\|_{\mathcal{I}}=o_{p}(1) and the factual probabilities of the mechanisms entering the target satisfy minj⁡αj≥ϵ>0\min_{j}\alpha_{j}\geq\epsilon>0, then

max⁡{|L^g​(A,a,v)−Lg​(A,a,v)|,|U^g​(A,a,v)−Ug​(A,a,v)|}=Op​(‖μ^−μ‖ℐ),\max\{|\widehat{L}_{g}(A,a;v)-L_{g}(A,a;v)|,|\widehat{U}_{g}(A,a;v)-U_{g}(A,a;v)|\}=O_{p}(\|\widehat{\mu}-\mu\|_{\mathcal{I}}),

uniformly over finite collections of interventions and scores.

5.2 Confidence intervals

Confidence intervals for partially identified parameters are constructed to cover the entire identified interval [Lg,Ug][L_{g},U_{g}] at nominal level 1−δ1-\delta (Imbens & Manski, 2004). Under independent sampling, simultaneous Clopper–Pearson intervals for the mm active probabilities are formed at level 1−δ/m1-\delta/m per coordinate (Clopper & Pearson, 1934). Replacing αj\alpha_{j} by its lower confidence limit αjL\alpha_{j}^{L} and μj​(w,p)\mu_{j}(w;p) by its upper confidence limit μjU​(w,p)\mu_{j}^{U}(w;p) relaxes the local constraint in (2) to αjL​q​(w)≤μjU​(w,p)\alpha_{j}^{L}q(w)\leq\mu_{j}^{U}(w;p) for p≠pj⋆p\neq p_{j}^{\star}. Optimizing Ψg​(q,A,a)\Psi_{g}(q;A,a) over the product of these enlarged simplices yields an outer simultaneous confidence interval [L~g,U~g][\widetilde{L}_{g},\widetilde{U}_{g}] with guaranteed finite-sample coverage (§ S4.3).

Proposition 3.

Under independent and identically distributed sampling, correctly specified causal and response restrictions, and pr⁡(V=v)>0\pr(V=v)>0,

pr{[Lg,Ug]⊆[L~g,U~g]}≥1−δ\pr\{[L_{g},U_{g}]\subseteq[\widetilde{L}_{g},\widetilde{U}_{g}]\}\geq 1-\delta

for every sample size. Simultaneous Gaussian or survey-design confidence regions for the active probabilities give asymptotic coverage at least 1−δ1-\delta by the same construction.

For asymptotic inference, let ℳ=∏jℳj\mathcal{M}=\prod_{j}\mathcal{M}_{j} and let ΠℳW\Pi_{\mathcal{M}}^{W} project each block using W=diag⁡(W1,…,Wd)W=\operatorname{diag}(W_{1},\ldots,W_{d}). Writing Lg​(A,a,v,η)L_{g}(A,a;v;\eta) and Ug​(A,a,v,η)U_{g}(A,a;v;\eta) for the sharp endpoints evaluated at compatible margins η∈ℳ\eta\in\mathcal{M}, define the composite endpoint map T⁡(η)={Lg​(A,a,v,ΠℳW​η),Ug​(A,a,v,ΠℳW​η)}TT(\eta)=\{L_{g}(A,a;v;\Pi_{\mathcal{M}}^{W}\eta),\,U_{g}(A,a;v;\Pi_{\mathcal{M}}^{W}\eta)\}^{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T}}. At parameters with positive active factual probabilities, this map is piecewise smooth and Hadamard directionally differentiable. Where its derivative is nonlinear, the standard plug-in bootstrap is inconsistent (Fang & Santos, 2019, Theorem 3.1).

Let μ~\widetilde{\mu} be an unprojected preliminary estimate, and let 𝔾n∗\mathbb{G}_{n}^{*} consistently approximate its centred Gaussian limit conditionally on the data. With εn→0\varepsilon_{n}\to 0 and n​εn→∞\sqrt{n}\varepsilon_{n}\to\infty, the directional difference quotient is

Zn∗=T⁡(μ~+εn​𝔾n∗)−T⁡(μ~)εn.Z_{n}^{*}=\frac{T(\widetilde{\mu}+\varepsilon_{n}\mathbb{G}_{n}^{*})-T(\widetilde{\mu})}{\varepsilon_{n}}.

Writing (L^g,U^g)T=T⁡(μ~)(\widehat{L}_{g},\widehat{U}_{g})^{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T}}=T(\widetilde{\mu}) and Zn∗=(ZL,n∗,ZU,n∗)TZ_{n}^{*}=(Z_{L,n}^{*},Z_{U,n}^{*})^{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T}}, let c^1−δ\widehat{c}_{1-\delta} denote the conditional (1−δ)(1-\delta) quantile of max⁡{ZL,n∗,−ZU,n∗}\max\{Z_{L,n}^{*},-Z_{U,n}^{*}\} given the data. This yields the confidence interval ℐ^g,n=[L^g−n−1/2max{0,c^1−δ},U^g+n−1/2max{0,c^1−δ}]\widehat{\mathcal{I}}_{g,n}=[\widehat{L}_{g}-n^{-1/2}\max\{0,\widehat{c}_{1-\delta}\},\,\allowbreak\widehat{U}_{g}+n^{-1/2}\max\{0,\widehat{c}_{1-\delta}\}] (§ S4.4; Hong & Li, 2018), whose asymptotic validity follows from directional differentiability of TT.

Proposition 4.

Suppose the state spaces and response sets are finite, μ∈ℳ\mu\in\mathcal{M} has positive factual probabilities for all mechanisms entering the target, and n(μ~−μ)→d𝔾μ∼N(0,Σμ)\sqrt{n}(\widetilde{\mu}-\mu)\to_{d}\mathbb{G}_{\mu}\sim N(0,\Sigma_{\mu}). Then TT is Hadamard directionally differentiable at μ\mu and n{T(μ~)−T(μ)}→dZ=(ZL,ZU)T=Tμ′(𝔾μ)\sqrt{n}\{T(\widetilde{\mu})-T(\mu)\}\to_{d}Z=(Z_{L},Z_{U})^{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T}}=T_{\mu}^{\prime}(\mathbb{G}_{\mu}). If the distribution function of max⁡{ZL,−ZU}\max\{Z_{L},-Z_{U}\} is continuous and strictly increasing at its (1−δ)(1-\delta) quantile, εn→0\varepsilon_{n}\to 0, n​εn→∞\sqrt{n}\varepsilon_{n}\to\infty, and the conditional multiplier law consistently estimates N⁡(0,Σμ)N(0,\Sigma_{\mu}), then

limn→∞pr{[Lg,Ug]⊆ℐ^g,n}≥1−δ.\lim_{n\to\infty}\pr\{[L_{g},U_{g}]\subseteq\widehat{\mathcal{I}}_{g,n}\}\geq 1-\delta.

6 Numerical illustrations

Synthetic reactor experiments and data from a national health survey illustrate exact bound computation, finite-sample estimation, and confidence interval performance.

6.1 Reactor example

In the five-variable Markovian reactor system depicted in Fig. 1(a), a binary cooling-valve fault A∈{0,1}A\in\{0,1\} affects temperature T∈{0,1,2}T\in\{0,1,2\}; temperature and an ordered feed deviation D∈{0,1,2}D\in\{0,1,2\} affect binary pressure P∈{0,1}P\in\{0,1\}; and (T,P)(T,P) govern shutdown severity Y∈{0,1,2}Y\in\{0,1,2\}. The population conditional distributions are specified in § S5.

For the observed incident v=(A,D,T,P,Y)=(1,2,2,1,2)v=(A,D,T,P,Y)=(1,2,2,1,2), which occurs with population probability 0.022680.02268, the posterior attribution effects τg​({A},0,v)\tau_{g}(\{A\},0;v) and τg​({D},0,v)\tau_{g}(\{D\},0;v) are evaluated using the severe-shutdown indicator score g⁡(y)=I⁡(y=2)g(y)=I(y=2). Because temperature TT belongs to the parent sets of both PP and YY, Proposition 2 yields the exact bounds by backward recursion with ℱ=∅\mathcal{F}=\emptyset, summarized in Table 1.

Cooling repair has a larger attribution effect than feed correction in every compatible model: its lower bound 0.67370.6737 exceeds the feed-correction upper bound 0.21600.2160 by 0.45770.4577. Table 1 also gives the pressure-mediated components and joint-repair bounds. Three compatible models with the same observational distribution attain the exact lower endpoint 382/567≈0.6737382/567\approx 0.6737, the independent-response value 19/25=0.760019/25=0.7600, and the exact upper endpoint 35/36≈0.972235/36\approx 0.9722 (§ S5.2).

For cooling repair, 20002000 independent datasets are generated at each sample size n∈{500,2000,8000}n\in\{500,2000,8000\} (Morris et al., 2019). Table 2 and Fig. 2 compare simultaneous Clopper–Pearson confidence intervals calibrated over all 2626 model probabilities or the 1212 active probabilities with the numerical directional method. The multiplier and estimation settings are detailed in § S5.4.

Calibration over the active probabilities reduces interval length while retaining 1.0001.000 empirical coverage. The numerical directional method reduces excess width by 73%73\% to 81%81\% across the three sample sizes, with empirical coverage increasing from 0.9360.936 at n=500n=500 to 0.9520.952 and 0.9570.957 at n=2000n=2000 and 80008000. At n=500n=500, fused least-squares estimation reduces both the magnitude of upper-endpoint bias and the root mean squared errors of both endpoints, with estimation errors decreasing at larger sample sizes. Complete bias, root mean squared error, paired mean squared error, and tuning results are reported in § S5.4.

6.2 Survey analysis

The 2017–2018 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey provides complete records on 55305530 adults aged at least 2020 years across 1515 masked strata and 3030 primary sampling units (Chen et al., 2020). The analysis uses interview weights. The variables follow the working causal ordering (X1,X2,X3,Y)(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3},Y), comprising recreational inactivity X1∈{0,1}X_{1}\in\{0,1\}, ordered self-rated diet X2∈{0,1,2}X_{2}\in\{0,1,2\} from excellent or very good to fair or poor, coronary heart disease history X3∈{0,1}X_{3}\in\{0,1\}, and hypertension diagnosis history Y∈{0,1,2}Y\in\{0,1,2\} with severe-outcome score g⁡(y)=I⁡(y=2)g(y)=I(y=2). The factual record v=(X1,X2,X3,Y)=(1,2,1,2)v=(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3},Y)=(1,2,1,2) is observed in 4242 participants, representing a survey-weighted proportion of 0.00490.0049, and the smallest active outcome parent cell contains 2323 observations with a Kish effective sample size of 9.89.8.

Table 3 compares four structural interventions. The lifestyle interventions modify behavioural exposures, whereas do⁡(X3=0)\mathrm{do}(X_{3}=0) sets the coronary heart disease indicator to zero prior to hypertension evaluation. Under do⁡(X3=0)\mathrm{do}(X_{3}=0), (X1,X2)=(1,2)(X_{1},X_{2})=(1,2) remains fixed, and the sharp interval [max⁡{0,1−βY/αY},min⁡{1,(1−βY)/αY}][\max\{0,1-\beta_{Y}/\alpha_{Y}\},\,\allowbreak\min\{1,(1-\beta_{Y})/\alpha_{Y}\}] depends only on αY=pr⁡(Y=2∣X1=1,X2=2,X3=1)\alpha_{Y}=\pr(Y=2\mid X_{1}=1,X_{2}=2,X_{3}=1) and βY=pr⁡(Y=2∣X1=1,X2=2,X3=0)\beta_{Y}=\pr(Y=2\mid X_{1}=1,X_{2}=2,X_{3}=0), estimated as 0.6820.682 and 0.3360.336 with plug-in interval [0.508,0.974][0.508,0.974]. Calibrating the simultaneous Gaussian region over (αY,βY)(\alpha_{Y},\beta_{Y}) narrows the 95% confidence interval from [0.000,1.000][0.000,1.000] under calibration over all 5454 non-root probabilities to [0.166,1.000][0.166,1.000], and Fieller inversion using the bivariate design covariance of (α^Y,β^Y)T(\widehat{\alpha}_{Y},\widehat{\beta}_{Y})^{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T}} for these two ratios yields [0.270,1.000][0.270,1.000]. The 95% simultaneous confidence region intersects the compatible margin set defined by the dietary monotonicity and unit-increment inequalities in (6); data processing, survey calibration, ratio inversion, and compatibility diagnostics are detailed in § S6.2.

7 Discussion

Conditioning on a complete factual record preserves independence across exogenous mechanisms in a Markovian structural causal model and reduces unrestricted nonfactual response constraints to explicit capped simplices. These feasible distributions combine through the realized response at each node into a single compatible model, establishing joint attainability and supporting exact backward recursion along causal chains and vertex enumeration across shared mechanisms in general directed acyclic graphs. Structural restrictions enter through compatible joint response distributions, whose polyhedral stability supports root-nn plug-in estimation and directional inference. Extending these results to partially observed intermediate records, dependent disturbances, or continuous responses requires optimization over coupled multi-node response laws or infinite-dimensional coupling sets.

Liyao Zhou and Xinwei Sun

S1 Proofs of posterior identification

S1.1 Proof of Theorem 1

Proof.

The conditional independence in Theorem 1(i) follows from nodewise exogenous independence. Under Assumption 1, the response vectors R1,…,RdR_{1},\ldots,R_{d} are mutually independent. The parent vector PjP_{j} is a function of R1,…,Rj−1R_{1},\ldots,R_{j-1} and is therefore independent of RjR_{j}. For each pp with pr⁡(Pj=p)>0\pr(P_{j}=p)>0, we have

pr(Vj=w∣Pj=p)=pr{Vj(p)=w∣Pj=p}=pr{Vj(p)=w}=μj(w;p),\pr(V_{j}=w\mid P_{j}=p)=\pr\{V_{j}(p)=w\mid P_{j}=p\}=\pr\{V_{j}(p)=w\}=\mu_{j}(w;p),

where the first equality holds by consistency and the second holds because PjP_{j} is independent of RjR_{j}. This proves the identification of μj​(w,p)\mu_{j}(w;p).

For the observed evidence V=vV=v, define Ej={Vj(pj⋆)=vj}E_{j}=\{V_{j}(p_{j}^{\star})=v_{j}\}. Then pr⁡(Ej)=αj\pr(E_{j})=\alpha_{j}. By recursive substitution in the structural equations, we have

{V=v}=⋂j=1dEj.\{V=v\}=\bigcap_{j=1}^{d}E_{j}.

Since each EjE_{j} depends only on RjR_{j}, the mutual independence of R1,…,RdR_{1},\ldots,R_{d} implies

pr⁡(V=v)=∏j=1dαj.\pr(V=v)=\prod_{j=1}^{d}\alpha_{j}.

Because pr⁡(V=v)>0\pr(V=v)>0, each αj\alpha_{j} is positive. For any subsets BjB_{j} of the response spaces, we then have

pr⁡(Rj∈Bj,j=1,…,d∣V=v)=∏j=1dpr⁡(Rj∈Bj,Ej)∏j=1dpr⁡(Ej)=∏j=1dpr⁡(Rj∈Bj∣Ej),\pr(R_{j}\in B_{j},\ j=1,\ldots,d\mid V=v)=\frac{\prod_{j=1}^{d}\pr(R_{j}\in B_{j},E_{j})}{\prod_{j=1}^{d}\pr(E_{j})}=\prod_{j=1}^{d}\pr(R_{j}\in B_{j}\mid E_{j}),

where the first equality follows from the independence of R1,…,RdR_{1},\ldots,R_{d} and the fact that EjE_{j} depends only on RjR_{j}. Therefore, the response vectors are mutually independent conditional on V=vV=v, as stated in part (i).

By consistency, qj​(pj⋆)=δvjq_{j}(p_{j}^{\star})=\delta_{v_{j}}. For p≠pj⋆p\neq p_{j}^{\star}, part (i) implies

αj​qj​(w,p)=pr⁡{Vj​(pj⋆)=vj,Vj​(p)=w}≤μj​(w,p).\alpha_{j}q_{j}(w;p)=\pr\{V_{j}(p_{j}^{\star})=v_{j},V_{j}(p)=w\}\leq\mu_{j}(w;p).

Thus qj​(p)q_{j}(p) satisfies the constraints defining 𝒦j​(p)\mathcal{K}_{j}(p) in (2). To complete parts (ii) and (iii), we show that all admissible conditional distributions can be attained simultaneously by a single compatible Markovian structural causal model.

For each jj and pp, choose qj​(p)∈𝒦j​(p)q_{j}(p)\in\mathcal{K}_{j}(p). When αj<1\alpha_{j}<1, define

rj​(w,p)=μj​(w,p)−αj​qj​(w,p)1−αj(p≠pj⋆).r_{j}(w;p)=\frac{\mu_{j}(w;p)-\alpha_{j}q_{j}(w;p)}{1-\alpha_{j}}\quad(p\neq p_{j}^{\star}).

The constraints on qj​(p)q_{j}(p) imply that rj​(w,p)≥0r_{j}(w;p)\geq 0 and ∑wrj​(w,p)=1\sum_{w}r_{j}(w;p)=1. We construct a joint distribution for RjR_{j} as follows. First, let Vj​(pj⋆)V_{j}(p_{j}^{\star}) have marginal distribution μj​(pj⋆)\mu_{j}(p_{j}^{\star}). Conditional on Vj​(pj⋆)=bV_{j}(p_{j}^{\star})=b, let the remaining responses {Vj​(p):p≠pj⋆}\{V_{j}(p):p\neq p_{j}^{\star}\} be mutually independent, with

pr⁡{Vj​(p)=w∣Vj​(pj⋆)=b}={qj​(w,p),b=vj,rj​(w,p),b≠vj.\pr\{V_{j}(p)=w\mid V_{j}(p_{j}^{\star})=b\}=\begin{cases}q_{j}(w;p),&b=v_{j},\\ r_{j}(w;p),&b\neq v_{j}.\end{cases}

By construction, for each p≠pj⋆p\neq p_{j}^{\star},

pr{Vj(p)=w}=αjqj(w;p)+(1−αj)rj(w;p)=μj(w;p).\pr\{V_{j}(p)=w\}=\alpha_{j}q_{j}(w;p)+(1-\alpha_{j})r_{j}(w;p)=\mu_{j}(w;p).

Moreover, conditioning on Vj​(pj⋆)=vjV_{j}(p_{j}^{\star})=v_{j} yields qj​(p)q_{j}(p) for every p≠pj⋆p\neq p_{j}^{\star}. When αj=1\alpha_{j}=1, the constraints imply qj​(p)=μj​(p)q_{j}(p)=\mu_{j}(p). In this case, we take the counterfactual responses to be mutually independent with these marginal distributions.

Finally, we take R1,…,RdR_{1},\ldots,R_{d} to be mutually independent with their respective constructed distributions, and define Uj=RjU_{j}=R_{j} and fj​(p,Uj)=Uj​(p)f_{j}(p,U_{j})=U_{j}(p). The resulting structural causal model satisfies Assumption 1 and has marginal response distributions {μj​(p)}\{\mu_{j}(p)\}. By part (i), its conditional response distributions given V=vV=v equal the selected qj​(p)q_{j}(p) for all jj and pp simultaneously. This establishes attainability in part (ii) and proves part (iii). ∎

S1.2 Proof of Theorem 2

Proof.

Let VaV_{a} denote the counterfactual vector under do⁡(A=a)\mathrm{do}(A=a); its conditional distribution given V=vV=v follows by causal recursion. Under do⁡(A=a)\mathrm{do}(A=a), the variables in AA are fixed at aa, and the remaining variables follow their structural equations. By Theorem 1(i), the response vector RjR_{j} is independent of the preceding response vectors conditional on V=vV=v. Successive conditioning in the causal order therefore gives

pr(Va=z∣V=v)=1{zA=a}∏j:Vj∉Aqj(zj;zPa⁡(Vj)).\pr(V_{a}=z\mid V=v)=1\{z_{A}=a\}\prod_{j:V_{j}\notin A}q_{j}(z_{j};z_{\Pa(V_{j})}). (S1)

If a preceding counterfactual event has probability zero, all its extensions also have probability zero, while the corresponding product vanishes by induction. Multiplying (S1) by g⁡(zY)g(z_{Y}) and summing over zz, we obtain E⁡{g⁡(Ya)∣V=v}=Ψg​(q,A,a)E\{g(Y_{a})\mid V=v\}=\Psi_{g}(q;A,a).

To establish sharpness, note that 𝒦A\mathcal{K}_{A} in (3) is the product of the sets 𝒦j​(p)\mathcal{K}_{j}(p) over the nonintervened variables and their parent configurations. By Theorem 1(iii), every q∈𝒦Aq\in\mathcal{K}_{A} can be attained by a compatible model. Moreover, 𝒦A\mathcal{K}_{A} is compact and connected, and Ψg​(⋅,A,a)\Psi_{g}(\cdot;A,a) is continuous. Therefore, the set of attainable values of E​{g⁡(Ya)∣V=v}E\{g(Y_{a})\mid V=v\} is the closed interval between the minimum and maximum of Ψg​(⋅,A,a)\Psi_{g}(\cdot;A,a) over 𝒦A\mathcal{K}_{A}. By consistency, the attribution effect in (1) equals g⁡(vY)−E⁡{g⁡(Ya)∣V=v}g(v_{Y})-E\{g(Y_{a})\mid V=v\}. Subtracting the upper and lower endpoints, respectively, from g⁡(vY)g(v_{Y}) completes the proof of Theorem 2. ∎

S1.3 Sharp bounds for posterior mediation effects

For the posterior mediation effects in § 3.2 of the main paper, let 𝒮\mathcal{S} denote the mediator nodes and M=V𝒮M=V_{\mathcal{S}} the corresponding vector. Consistency gives MvA=vMM_{v_{A}}=v_{M} conditional on {V=v}\{V=v\} and Ya,Ma=YaY_{a,M_{a}}=Y_{a}, so

τgTNDE\displaystyle\tau_{g}^{\mathrm{TNDE}} =g⁡(vY)−Ψg​(q,A∪𝒮,(a,vM)),\displaystyle=g(v_{Y})-\Psi_{g}(q;A\cup\mathcal{S},(a,v_{M})),
τgPNIE\displaystyle\tau_{g}^{\mathrm{PNIE}} =Ψg​(q,A∪𝒮,(a,vM))−Ψg​(q,A,a).\displaystyle=\Psi_{g}(q;A\cup\mathcal{S},(a,v_{M}))-\Psi_{g}(q;A,a).

Both counterfactual expectations are evaluated using the same q∈𝒦Aq\in\mathcal{K}_{A}. The conditional response distributions of the mediators do not enter the first expectation, since their values are fixed at vMv_{M}.

For fixed values of the other conditional distributions, each expectation is affine in qj​(p)q_{j}(p), because each term in the corresponding factorization contains at most one response probability from mechanism jj. Their difference has the same property, so each objective attains its minimum and maximum at a product of vertices of the sets 𝒦j​(p)\mathcal{K}_{j}(p). By Theorem 1(iii), each such selection is attainable by a compatible model. Continuity of the objectives and connectedness of 𝒦A\mathcal{K}_{A} then imply that every value between the respective endpoints is attainable. For the pure natural indirect effect, the difference is optimized over a common qq; separate extrema of the two expectations can be attained by different distributions. This proves sharpness for both mediated effects.

For a single mediator M=VmM=V_{m}, with 𝒮={Vm}\mathcal{S}=\{V_{m}\}, consider the total natural indirect effect τgTNIE=g⁡(vY)−E⁡{g⁡(YvA,Ma)∣V=v}\tau_{g}^{\mathrm{TNIE}}=g(v_{Y})-E\{g(Y_{v_{A},M_{a}})\mid V=v\}. The counterfactual MaM_{a} depends only on the response vectors of VmV_{m} and its ancestors. On {V=v}\{V=v\}, under do⁡(A=vA,Vm=w)\mathrm{do}(A=v_{A},V_{m}=w), every variable other than VmV_{m} that is not a descendant of VmV_{m} retains its factual value. Hence YvA,wY_{v_{A},w} depends only on the response vectors of descendants of VmV_{m}. By Theorem 1(i), Ma⟂YvA,w|V=vM_{a}\perp Y_{v_{A},w}\mid V=v for every w∈𝒳mw\in\mathcal{X}_{m}. Consequently,

E⁡{g⁡(YvA,Ma)∣V=v}=∑w∈𝒳mpr⁡(Ma=w∣V=v)​Ψg​(q,A∪{Vm},(vA,w)).E\{g(Y_{v_{A},M_{a}})\mid V=v\}=\sum_{w\in\mathcal{X}_{m}}\pr(M_{a}=w\mid V=v)\Psi_{g}(q;A\cup\{V_{m}\},(v_{A},w)). (S2)

By (S1), each factor in every summand is affine in each conditional distribution separately. Since the two factors involve disjoint sets of mechanisms, their product, and hence the sum, is also affine in each qj​(p)q_{j}(p) separately.

Lemma S1 (Block-ordered multimediator total natural indirect effect).

Let 𝒮⊆𝒱∖(A∪{Y})\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{V}\setminus(A\cup\{Y\}), M=V𝒮M=V_{\mathcal{S}}, and

𝒲=(𝒱∖(A∪𝒮))∩Desc⁡(𝒮).\mathcal{W}=(\mathcal{V}\setminus(A\cup\mathcal{S}))\cap\operatorname{Desc}(\mathcal{S}).

Here Desc⁡(𝒮)\operatorname{Desc}(\mathcal{S}) denotes the set of descendants of nodes in 𝒮\mathcal{S}. Suppose no node in 𝒮\mathcal{S} is a descendant of a node in 𝒲\mathcal{W}. Under Assumption 1 and complete factual conditioning, for every m∈𝒳𝒮m\in\mathcal{X}_{\mathcal{S}}, Ma⟂YvA,m|V=vM_{a}\perp Y_{v_{A},m}\mid V=v, and

E⁡{g⁡(YvA,Ma)∣V=v}=∑m∈𝒳𝒮pr⁡(Ma=m∣V=v)​Ψg​(q,A∪𝒮,(vA,m)).E\{g(Y_{v_{A},M_{a}})\mid V=v\}=\sum_{m\in\mathcal{X}_{\mathcal{S}}}\pr(M_{a}=m\mid V=v)\Psi_{g}(q;A\cup\mathcal{S},(v_{A},m)).

This functional is affine in each conditional response distribution separately. Its extrema over 𝒦A\mathcal{K}_{A} give the sharp interval for τgTNIE\tau_{g}^{\mathrm{TNIE}} after subtraction from g⁡(vY)g(v_{Y}).

Proof.

The counterfactual MaM_{a} is determined by response vectors at mediator nodes and their nonintervened ancestors. The block-ordering condition places all these mechanisms outside 𝒲\mathcal{W}. Under do⁡(A=vA,M=m)\mathrm{do}(A=v_{A},M=m), nodes outside 𝒮∪𝒲\mathcal{S}\cup\mathcal{W} retain their factual values, so YvA,mY_{v_{A},m} depends only on response vectors indexed by 𝒲\mathcal{W}. Theorem 1(i) gives the stated conditional independence and decomposition. The two factors in each summand involve disjoint mechanisms and are separately affine in each conditional response distribution, so their product and sum have the same property. Theorem 1(iii) gives simultaneous attainment of the optimizing conditional distributions; continuity and connectedness of 𝒦A\mathcal{K}_{A} give attainment of every intermediate value. ∎

S1.4 Binary monotonicity and proof of Corollary 1

The binary identification formula in § 3.1 of the main paper follows from the response restrictions. Suppose vX=1v_{X}=1, the exposure and all its descendants are binary, and each affected structural mechanism is coordinatewise nondecreasing in its affected parents. Under do⁡(X=0)\mathrm{do}(X=0), induction in the causal order shows that each counterfactual variable Vj,0V_{j,0} satisfies Vj,0≤vjV_{j,0}\leq v_{j}. For each affected node VjV_{j} and reachable parent configuration p≤pj⋆p\leq p_{j}^{\star}, monotonicity implies {Vj(p)=1}⊆{Vj(pj⋆)=1}\{V_{j}(p)=1\}\subseteq\{V_{j}(p_{j}^{\star})=1\}. Therefore, by Theorem 1(i),

qj​(1,p)=pr⁡{Vj​(p)=1∣Vj​(pj⋆)=vj}={0,vj=0,μj​(1,p)/αj,vj=1.q_{j}(1;p)=\pr\{V_{j}(p)=1\mid V_{j}(p_{j}^{\star})=v_{j}\}=\begin{cases}0,&v_{j}=0,\\ \mu_{j}(1;p)/\alpha_{j},&v_{j}=1.\end{cases}
Proof.

Let 𝟏\boldsymbol{1} and 𝟎\boldsymbol{0} denote vectors of ones and zeros of the required dimensions. For the observed evidence V=𝟏V=\boldsymbol{1} and intervention do⁡(A=𝟎A)\mathrm{do}(A=\boldsymbol{0}_{A}), let q⋆q^{\star} collect the binary conditional distributions with qj⋆​(1,p)=μj​(1,p)/αjq_{j}^{\star}(1;p)=\mu_{j}(1;p)/\alpha_{j} for every jj and pp. Because the marginal distributions are compatible with nondecreasing mechanisms, qj⋆​(1,p)q_{j}^{\star}(1;p) is nondecreasing in pp. Moreover, the constraints on 𝒦A\mathcal{K}_{A} imply qj​(1,p)≤qj⋆​(1,p)q_{j}(1;p)\leq q_{j}^{\star}(1;p) for every q∈𝒦Aq\in\mathcal{K}_{A}.

To compare the counterfactual outcomes under qq and q⋆q^{\star}, use independent uniform random variables at the nonintervened nodes, with the same draw shared between the two constructions at each node. Each response is one if this draw does not exceed the corresponding conditional success probability. For parent configurations p≤p′p\leq p^{\prime}, we have

qj​(1,p)≤qj⋆​(1,p)≤qj⋆​(1,p′).q_{j}(1;p)\leq q_{j}^{\star}(1;p)\leq q_{j}^{\star}(1;p^{\prime}).

Thus, if the preceding variables under qq are no larger than those under q⋆q^{\star}, the same ordering holds at the current node. Induction along the causal order gives the ordering of the outcomes and hence Ψg​(q,A,a)≤Ψg​(q⋆,A,a)\Psi_{g}(q;A,a)\leq\Psi_{g}(q^{\star};A,a).

It remains to show that structural monotonicity identifies q⋆q^{\star} and that q⋆q^{\star} is attainable. Since V=𝟏V=\boldsymbol{1}, every parent configuration satisfies p≤pj⋆p\leq p_{j}^{\star}. Under structural monotonicity, Vj​(p)≤Vj​(pj⋆)V_{j}(p)\leq V_{j}(p_{j}^{\star}) almost surely. By Theorem 1(i), every compatible monotone model therefore satisfies qj​(1,p)=μj​(1,p)/αj=qj⋆​(1,p)q_{j}(1;p)=\mu_{j}(1;p)/\alpha_{j}=q_{j}^{\star}(1;p). To establish attainability, let U1,…,UdU_{1},\ldots,U_{d} be independent uniform random variables on (0,1)(0,1) and define Vj(p)=1{Uj≤μj(1;p)}V_{j}(p)=1\{U_{j}\leq\mu_{j}(1;p)\}. These structural equations are nondecreasing in pp, have the required marginal distributions, and induce q⋆q^{\star} conditional on V=𝟏V=\boldsymbol{1}. Thus structural monotonicity identifies the counterfactual success probability at its unrestricted maximum, so τmono​(A,a,𝟏)=Lg​(A,a,𝟏)\tau_{\mathrm{mono}}(A,a;\boldsymbol{1})=L_{g}(A,a;\boldsymbol{1}). ∎

S2 Structural restrictions

S2.1 Proof of Theorem 3

For the allowed response vectors 𝒞j\mathcal{C}_{j} in the main paper, define

𝒢j={πj∈Δ(𝒞j):∑r∈𝒞j:r⁡(p)=wπj(r)=μj(w;p),p∈𝒫j,w∈𝒳j},\mathcal{G}_{j}=\left\{\pi_{j}\in\Delta(\mathcal{C}_{j}):\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}r\in\mathcal{C}_{j}:\\ r(p)=w\end{subarray}}\pi_{j}(r)=\mu_{j}(w;p),\quad p\in\mathcal{P}_{j},\;w\in\mathcal{X}_{j}\right\}, (S3)

assumed nonempty for each j=1,…,dj=1,\ldots,d. Write 𝒢j​(ηj)\mathcal{G}_{j}(\eta_{j}) for this set with marginal table ηj\eta_{j}. Conditioning on Vj​(pj⋆)=vjV_{j}(p_{j}^{\star})=v_{j} updates πj∈𝒢j\pi_{j}\in\mathcal{G}_{j} to αj−11{r(pj⋆)=vj}πj(r)\alpha_{j}^{-1}1\{r(p_{j}^{\star})=v_{j}\}\pi_{j}(r) and induces the set of conditional response distributions

𝒬j={{qj(p)}p∈𝒫j:qj(w;p)=1αj∑r∈𝒞j:r⁡(pj⋆)=vj,r⁡(p)=wπj(r),πj∈𝒢j},\mathcal{Q}_{j}=\left\{\{q_{j}(p)\}_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{j}}:q_{j}(w;p)=\frac{1}{\alpha_{j}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}r\in\mathcal{C}_{j}:\\ r(p_{j}^{\star})=v_{j},\;r(p)=w\end{subarray}}\pi_{j}(r),\quad\pi_{j}\in\mathcal{G}_{j}\right\},

with joint domain 𝒬A=∏j:Vj∉A𝒬j\mathcal{Q}_{A}=\prod_{j:V_{j}\notin A}\mathcal{Q}_{j}.

Proof.

For any compatible model, let πj\pi_{j} denote the distribution of RjR_{j}. Then πj∈𝒢j\pi_{j}\in\mathcal{G}_{j} in (S3). By Theorem 1(i), we have

pr(Rj=r∣V=v)=αj−11{r(pj⋆)=vj}πj(r).\pr(R_{j}=r\mid V=v)=\alpha_{j}^{-1}1\{r(p_{j}^{\star})=v_{j}\}\pi_{j}(r).

Marginalizing this posterior distribution over the response coordinates yields a collection of conditional distributions in 𝒬j\mathcal{Q}_{j}. By (S1), we therefore have E⁡{g⁡(Ya)∣V=v}=Ψg​(q,A,a)E\{g(Y_{a})\mid V=v\}=\Psi_{g}(q;A,a) for some q∈𝒬Aq\in\mathcal{Q}_{A}.

Conversely, consider any q∈𝒬Aq\in\mathcal{Q}_{A}. For each nonintervened variable, the definition of 𝒬j\mathcal{Q}_{j} ensures that there exists πj∈𝒢j\pi_{j}\in\mathcal{G}_{j} inducing the selected qjq_{j} through the posterior projection defining 𝒬j\mathcal{Q}_{j}. For each intervened variable, choose any πj∈𝒢j\pi_{j}\in\mathcal{G}_{j}. We construct independent response vectors with these distributions and set Uj=RjU_{j}=R_{j} and fj​(p,Uj)=Uj​(p)f_{j}(p,U_{j})=U_{j}(p). The resulting structural causal model satisfies Assumption 1 and the response restrictions, and has the required marginal response distributions. By Theorem 1(i), it induces the selected qq conditional on V=vV=v.

Each 𝒬j\mathcal{Q}_{j} is a linear image of the nonempty compact convex polytope 𝒢j\mathcal{G}_{j}. Thus 𝒬A\mathcal{Q}_{A} is compact and connected. As in the proof of Theorem 2, continuity of Ψg​(⋅,A,a)\Psi_{g}(\cdot;A,a) implies that every value between its minimum and maximum is attained. This proves Theorem 3. ∎

S2.2 Proof of Proposition 1

Proof.

For a fixed mechanism jj and configuration ss of the remaining parents, write Wk=Vj​(s,xk)W_{k}=V_{j}(s,x_{k}) for k=0,…,Kk=0,\ldots,K. The distribution function of WkW_{k} is Fj​(⋅,s,xk)F_{j}(\cdot;s,x_{k}), as defined in the main paper. Necessity follows directly from the response restrictions in (5). The restrictions 0≤Wk+1−Wk≤bj​k0\leq W_{k+1}-W_{k}\leq b_{jk} imply

{Wk≤r−bj​k}⊆{Wk+1≤r}⊆{Wk≤r}.\{W_{k}\leq r-b_{jk}\}\subseteq\{W_{k+1}\leq r\}\subseteq\{W_{k}\leq r\}.

Taking probabilities gives the inequalities in (6).

For sufficiency, construct a joint distribution satisfying the response restrictions when these inequalities hold. For 0<u<10<u<1, define

Qk​(u)=min⁡{r∈{0,…,Mj}:Fj​(r,s,xk)≥u}.Q_{k}(u)=\min\{r\in\{0,\ldots,M_{j}\}:F_{j}(r;s,x_{k})\geq u\}.

The inequalities in (6) imply Qk​(u)≤Qk+1​(u)≤Qk​(u)+bj​kQ_{k}(u)\leq Q_{k+1}(u)\leq Q_{k}(u)+b_{jk}. Let UU be uniform on (0,1)(0,1) and set Wk=Qk​(U)W_{k}=Q_{k}(U) for every kk. Each WkW_{k} then has distribution function Fj​(⋅,s,xk)F_{j}(\cdot;s,x_{k}), and the adjacent-increment restrictions hold simultaneously. Taking these quantile couplings independently across different ss gives a joint response distribution in 𝒢j\mathcal{G}_{j}, which proves sufficiency. ∎

S2.3 Restrictions relative to the observed response

In § 3.3 of the main paper, each restricted response under restrictions relative to the observed response is compared only with the response at the observed parent configuration. The following lemma shows that the resulting conditional distributions can be selected separately across parent configurations and attained simultaneously.

Lemma S2 (Couplings with a common factual response).

For mechanism jj, suppose the only response restrictions are Vj​(p)≤Vj​(pj⋆)V_{j}(p)\leq V_{j}(p_{j}^{\star}) for p∈ℰj⊆𝒫j∖{pj⋆}p\in\mathcal{E}_{j}\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{j}\setminus\{p_{j}^{\star}\}. For each p≠pj⋆p\neq p_{j}^{\star}, choose a bivariate distribution for {Vj​(pj⋆),Vj​(p)}\{V_{j}(p_{j}^{\star}),V_{j}(p)\} with margins μj​(pj⋆)\mu_{j}(p_{j}^{\star}) and μj​(p)\mu_{j}(p), supported on {w≤z}\{w\leq z\} when p∈ℰjp\in\mathcal{E}_{j}. Then there exists a joint distribution of RjR_{j} in 𝒢j\mathcal{G}_{j} with all the chosen bivariate margins. If αj>0\alpha_{j}>0, the corresponding conditional distributions given Vj​(pj⋆)=vjV_{j}(p_{j}^{\star})=v_{j} can therefore be selected separately and attained simultaneously, so that 𝒬j=∏p∈𝒫j𝒬j​(p)\mathcal{Q}_{j}=\prod_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{j}}\mathcal{Q}_{j}(p).

Proof.

Let γp​(z,w)\gamma_{p}(z,w) denote the chosen bivariate probability mass function for {Vj​(pj⋆),Vj​(p)}\{V_{j}(p_{j}^{\star}),V_{j}(p)\} at parent configuration p≠pj⋆p\neq p_{j}^{\star}. Let Vj​(pj⋆)V_{j}(p_{j}^{\star}) have marginal distribution μj​(pj⋆)\mu_{j}(p_{j}^{\star}). Conditional on Vj​(pj⋆)=zV_{j}(p_{j}^{\star})=z with μj​(z,pj⋆)>0\mu_{j}(z;p_{j}^{\star})>0, let the remaining responses Vj​(p)V_{j}(p) (p≠pj⋆p\neq p_{j}^{\star}) be mutually independent, with

pr⁡{Vj​(p)=w∣Vj​(pj⋆)=z}=γp​(z,w)μj​(z,pj⋆).\pr\{V_{j}(p)=w\mid V_{j}(p_{j}^{\star})=z\}=\frac{\gamma_{p}(z,w)}{\mu_{j}(z;p_{j}^{\star})}.

For values of zz with zero marginal probability, the conditional distributions can be chosen arbitrarily on {w≤z}\{w\leq z\}. By construction, each pair {Vj​(pj⋆),Vj​(p)}\{V_{j}(p_{j}^{\star}),V_{j}(p)\} has the chosen bivariate distribution γp\gamma_{p}. Thus the joint distribution belongs to 𝒢j\mathcal{G}_{j}, satisfies all the restrictions relative to the observed response, and simultaneously attains the selected conditional distributions at z=vjz=v_{j}. ∎

For an ordinal outcome with state space 𝒳Y={0,…,MY}\mathcal{X}_{Y}=\{0,\ldots,M_{Y}\}, consider the threshold probabilities θr=pr⁡(Ya<r∣V=v)\theta_{r}=\pr(Y_{a}<r\mid V=v), with the intervention and observed evidence fixed. S4.4 Proof of Proposition 4 and implementation details

Proof.

Write 𝒢j​(ηj)\mathcal{G}_{j}(\eta_{j}) in standard form, including normalization, and remove redundant equalities. Each vertex is affine in ηj\eta_{j} on a polyhedral feasibility region, with finitely many bases. The counterfactual expectation is linear in each joint response law separately, so the endpoints are attained at products of such vertices. Substitution gives finitely many rational functions with denominators that are products of positive factual probabilities. They are continuously differentiable near μ\mu.

For a direction hh in the tangent cone of ℳ\mathcal{M} at μ\mu, the feasible bases are constant along μ+t​h\mu+th for sufficiently small t>0t>0. Differences between candidate values have numerators that are either identically zero or have finitely many zeros near zero. Hence each endpoint follows a fixed differentiable candidate along this ray. The local Lipschitz bound in § S4.2 makes these directional limits stable under converging directions: the difference of the corresponding quotients is bounded by C​‖hn−h‖C\|h_{n}-h\|.

The projection ΠℳW\Pi_{\mathcal{M}}^{W} is piecewise affine and Hadamard directionally differentiable. Its derivative lies in the tangent cone. Composing this projection with the directional endpoint limits proves directional differentiability of TT, with Tμ′​(h)T_{\mu}^{\prime}(h) obtained by evaluating the endpoint derivative in the projected direction (ΠℳW)μ′​(h)(\Pi_{\mathcal{M}}^{W})^{\prime}_{\mu}(h). The directional delta method gives

n{T(μ~)−T(μ)}→dZ=(ZL,ZU)T=Tμ′(𝔾μ)\sqrt{n}\{T(\widetilde{\mu})-T(\mu)\}\to_{d}Z=(Z_{L},Z_{U})^{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T}}=T_{\mu}^{\prime}(\mathbb{G}_{\mu})

(Fang & Santos, 2019, Theorem 2.1).

For any compact set KK of directions, local Lipschitz continuity gives

suph∈K‖T⁡(μ~+εn​h)−T⁡(μ~)εn−T⁡(μ+εn​h)−T⁡(μ)εn‖≤2​C​‖μ~−μ‖εn=op​(1).\sup_{h\in K}\left\|\frac{T(\widetilde{\mu}+\varepsilon_{n}h)-T(\widetilde{\mu})}{\varepsilon_{n}}-\frac{T(\mu+\varepsilon_{n}h)-T(\mu)}{\varepsilon_{n}}\right\|\leq\frac{2C\|\widetilde{\mu}-\mu\|}{\varepsilon_{n}}=o_{p}(1).

Hadamard directional differentiability makes the second quotient converge uniformly on compact sets to Tμ′​(h)T_{\mu}^{\prime}(h). Conditional tightness and consistency of 𝔾n∗\mathbb{G}_{n}^{*} therefore give conditional weak convergence of Zn∗Z_{n}^{*} to ZZ (Hong & Li, 2018). The stated quantile conditions yield consistency of c^1−δ\widehat{c}_{1-\delta} and the coverage conclusion. ∎

Covariance estimation and multiplier implementation. Write (L^g,U^g)T=T⁡(μ~)(\widehat{L}_{g},\widehat{U}_{g})^{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T}}=T(\widetilde{\mu}) and Zn∗=(ZL,n∗,ZU,n∗)TZ_{n}^{*}=(Z_{L,n}^{*},Z_{U,n}^{*})^{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T}}. S5.4 Simulation design and complete Monte Carlo results

For each sample size n∈{500,2000,8000}n\in\{500,2000,8000\}, we generate 20002000 independent datasets with random seed 20261014 and report Monte Carlo standard errors following Morris et al. (2019). The conditional distributions of TT given AA and YY given (T,P)(T,P) are estimated by empirical frequencies, while pr⁡(P∣T,D)\pr(P\mid T,D) is estimated either by empirical frequencies or by five-fold cross-validated fused least squares with fixed penalty JP​(ηP)=(1/3)​∑t=02∑d=01‖ηP​(t,d+1)−ηP​(t,d)‖1J_{P}(\eta_{P})=(1/3)\sum_{t=0}^{2}\sum_{d=0}^{1}\|\eta_{P}(t,d+1)-\eta_{P}(t,d)\|_{1} over tuning grids γn=c​n−β\gamma_{n}=cn^{-\beta} with β∈{1/2,3/4}\beta\in\{1/2,3/4\} and c∈{0,0.05,0.10,0.20,0.50}c\in\{0,0.05,0.10,0.20,0.50\}. In each replicate, observations are partitioned randomly into five equal-sized folds; for each candidate cc, the piecewise-quadratic fused least-squares objective (S4) is solved to a convergence tolerance of 10−1010^{-10}, the coefficient c^\widehat{c} minimizing the held-out unpenalized Brier loss is selected, and pr⁡(P∣T,D)\pr(P\mid T,D) is refitted on the full sample at γ^n=c^​n−β\widehat{\gamma}_{n}=\widehat{c}n^{-\beta}. For directional inference, 800800 Gaussian multiplier draws 𝔾n∗∼N⁡(0,Σ^μ)\mathbb{G}_{n}^{*}\sim N(0,\widehat{\Sigma}_{\mu}) with random seed 20280085 are generated using the plug-in multinomial covariance Σ^μ\widehat{\Sigma}_{\mu} evaluated at the empirical frequencies.

The numerical directional intervals use εn=n−1/3\varepsilon_{n}=n^{-1/3}. At n=500n=500, fusion with rate n−3/4n^{-3/4} reduces the lower- and upper-endpoint root mean squared errors from 4.19×10−24.19\times 10^{-2} and 2.78×10−22.78\times 10^{-2} to 4.05×10−24.05\times 10^{-2} and 2.51×10−22.51\times 10^{-2}. At n=2000n=2000, its paired upper-endpoint mean squared error reduction is 7.29×10−67.29\times 10^{-6} (Monte Carlo standard error 1.19×10−61.19\times 10^{-6}).

Tables S2–S5 and Fig. S1 present the endpoint estimation errors, paired mean squared error differences, cross-validation selection frequencies, and complete confidence interval diagnostics.

S6.2 NHANES analysis details

In the 2017–2018 NHANES analysis of § 6.2, we merge the files DEMO_J, PAQ_J, DBQ_J, MCQ_J, and BPQ_J by participant identifier SEQN for adults aged at least 2020 years. Recreational inactivity X1∈{0,1}X_{1}\in\{0,1\} sets X1=1X_{1}=1 for participants answering no (2) to both vigorous (PAQ650) and moderate (PAQ665) recreational activity, and X1=0X_{1}=0 otherwise. Self-rated diet X2∈{0,1,2}X_{2}\in\{0,1,2\} from DBQ700 codes excellent or very good (1,2) as 00, good (3) as 11, and fair or poor (4,5) as 22. Coronary heart disease history X3∈{0,1}X_{3}\in\{0,1\} from MCQ160C codes yes (1) as 11 and no (2) as 00. Hypertension diagnosis history Y∈{0,1,2}Y\in\{0,1,2\} from BPQ020 and BPQ030 codes never told of hypertension (BPQ020=2) as Y=0Y=0, told only once (BPQ020=1 and BPQ030=2) as Y=1Y=1, and told on two or more visits (BPQ020=1 and BPQ030=1) as Y=2Y=2. Participants with refused (7) or don’t know (9) responses on any of these items are excluded, yielding the complete-case sample of n=5530n=5530 adults.

Survey variance and confidence calibration. Survey-weighted marginal proportions μ~\widetilde{\mu} and their Taylor-linearized design covariance matrix Σ^surv\widehat{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{surv}} are computed using interview weights WTINT2YR, 1515 masked variance strata (SDMVSTRA), and 3030 primary sampling units (SDMVPSU), providing 30−15=1530-15=15 design degrees of freedom (Chen et al., 2020). For each intervention (A,a)(A,a) in Table S1, let Σ^act\widehat{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{act}} denote the m×mm\times m submatrix of Σ^surv\widehat{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{surv}} on ℐ\mathcal{I}. We generate 150,000150{,}000 draws from N⁡(0,Σ^act)N(0,\widehat{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{act}}) with random seed 20261014 to calibrate the 95%95\% simultaneous critical value c0.95actc_{0.95}^{\mathrm{act}} of the maximum standardized deviation across the mm coordinates, which reduces c0.95actc_{0.95}^{\mathrm{act}} from 3.18163.1816 (mcal=54m_{\mathrm{cal}}=54) to 2.23512.2351 (m=2m=2 for do⁡(X3=0)\mathrm{do}(X_{3}=0)).

For do⁡(X3=0)\mathrm{do}(X_{3}=0) at v=(1,2,1,2)v=(1,2,1,2), the active outcome probabilities are αY=pr⁡(Y=2∣X1=1,X2=2,X3=1)\alpha_{Y}=\pr(Y=2\mid X_{1}=1,X_{2}=2,X_{3}=1) and βY=pr⁡(Y=2∣X1=1,X2=2,X3=0)\beta_{Y}=\pr(Y=2\mid X_{1}=1,X_{2}=2,X_{3}=0), with survey-weighted point estimates α^Y=0.681956\widehat{\alpha}_{Y}=0.681956 and β^Y=0.335808\widehat{\beta}_{Y}=0.335808, giving the plug-in sharp interval [max⁡(0,1−β^Y/α^Y),min⁡{1,(1−β^Y)/α^Y}]=[0.5076,0.9740][\max(0,1-\widehat{\beta}_{Y}/\widehat{\alpha}_{Y}),\,\min\{1,(1-\widehat{\beta}_{Y})/\widehat{\alpha}_{Y}\}]=[0.5076,0.9740]. S6.3 Additional examples on ordinal exposures and network attribution

Two further examples illustrate bounded adjacent increments for an ordinal exposure and multi-parent attribution in an engineering reliability network.

First, consider a two-variable system X→YX\to Y with ordered exposure X∈{x0<x1<x2}X\in\{x_{0}<x_{1}<x_{2}\}, outcome Y∈{0,1,2}Y\in\{0,1,2\}, score g⁡(y)=yg(y)=y, factual record (X,Y)=(x2,2)(X,Y)=(x_{2},2), and intervention do⁡(X=x0)\mathrm{do}(X=x_{0}).
